title: Learning Actionable Information Landscapes for Multimodal Active Sensing in Hawkmoths
claim: Two embodied sensing tasks are defined by their environments, a shared generative model of actions and observations, and multimodal sensory inputs.
layout: 2 stacked rows of 3 panels each, left-to-right, color-coded green and blue
description: The figure has two horizontal rounded boxes. The top box, in green, is labeled Nectary search. The bottom box, in blue, is labeled Flower tracking. Each row has three panels. In the top row, panel (a) shows a flower and moth schematic, with four flower geometry surfaces (funnel, near-funnel, near-flat, flat) and four gray-patterned flower patterns. abstract: Animals integrate information across sensory modalities to guide exploration, suggesting that they maintain internal estimates of where actions are expected to reduce uncertainty. However, how such action-conditioned information maps are learned from multimodal sensory experience remains unclear, as previous studies have been largely confined to unimodal sensing frameworks. We introduce a multimodal predictive-coding framework for learning uncertainty-reduction maps from visual and mechanosensory observations in hawkmoth flower interaction tasks. A variational generative model trained on simulated environments recovers modality-specific information landscapes over the action space, capturing how visual patterns, surface geometry, and mechanosensory cues shape the value of exploratory actions. These learned maps are consistent with several features of hawkmoth behavior, including nonzero tracking offsets, probing along visual patterns, and geometry-dependent exploration. Applying the model to behavioral data from flower tracking and nectary search, we find that natural trajectories tend to occupy regions of high uncertainty reduction in these learned maps. Building on these observations, we develop an uncertainty-gated lexicographic algorithm that switches between information gathering and reward exploitation based on perceptual uncertainty. In nectary search, uncertainty gating improves learning relative to exploit-only, $Îµ$-greedy, fixed-time, and uncertainty-calibrated non-lexicographic controls, with better generalization and robustness to sensory and curvature shifts. These results link information landscapes learned through generative modeling to biological sensing and embodied exploration.
